analysis.one_liner: Phases out sales of new gas-powered passenger vehicles, requiring only zero-emission cars by 2035.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with just one cosponsor in the Senate's final two weeks, never left the Environment and Public Works Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The ZEVs Act would have created a national zero-emission vehicle standard under the Clean Air Act. Starting in model year 2026, each automaker would have had to deliver at least 35% zero-emission vehicles for sale, rising every year until 2035, when only zero-emission cars could be sold. Automakers falling short could buy or trade credits or pay civil penalties worth twice the value of the credits they missed.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone exposed to tailpipe pollution — city residents, people living near highways, and children — would gain cleaner air as new gas-powered cars are phased out, and the country would cut greenhouse gas emissions from its largest light-duty source. Automakers that already build electric vehicles would gain a new revenue stream selling zero-emission credits to slower-moving competitors. Electric utilities and charging companies would gain from increased demand.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People breathing tailpipe pollution; EV-making automakers

how_it_helps.text: Sets an escalating national floor on zero-emission vehicle sales — 35% of each manufacturer's new passenger vehicles in model year 2026, rising in annual steps to 100% by model year 2035, after which only zero-emission vehicles could be sold.
Because the standard applies to every vehicle sold in the United States, it would cut smog-forming and climate-warming exhaust nationwide rather than only in states that adopt their own standards.

Creates a tradeable credit market so automakers that outperform the standard can sell credits to laggards, and imposes civil penalties equal to twice the value of any missing credits, deposited into the Highway Trust Fund.
Explicitly preserves states' authority to set stricter emissions and zero-emission vehicle rules of their own, so California-style programs could continue on top of the national floor.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers that keep selling mostly gas-powered cars would bear the costs: buying credits from competitors, paying civil penalties, and retooling their fleets for electric models — costs they would likely pass on to new-car buyers through higher prices. Oil refiners and fuel retailers would face shrinking gasoline demand as the phase-out proceeds. Consumers in areas with limited charging access or affordable electric models would bear transition frictions the bill does not directly address.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gas-vehicle automakers, oil refiners, some car buyers

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes its mandate entirely on manufacturers, with no consumer subsidies, affordability provisions, or charging-infrastructure funding in the text; its only nod to buyers is a nonbinding 'sense of Congress' that manufacturers diversify models to ensure consumer choice.

Compliance costs would fall on manufacturers first — civil penalties set at twice the value of missing credits — and manufacturers would likely recover them through higher new-vehicle prices, hitting buyers hardest in the early years of the ramp.

The credit-trading design lets a lagging automaker buy its way into compliance instead of actually selling more electric vehicles, which could slow the real-world shift in what sits on dealer lots even while the percentages are met on paper.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and durable: cleaner air for everyone and a binding end date for new gas-car sales, phased over a decade so manufacturers have time to convert. The credit market and penalty structure give laggards flexibility, but that same flexibility means the earliest years could be met partly through credit purchases rather than actual electric sales, and the bill asks consumers to absorb higher prices and charging gaps without offering them anything directly. A well-designed bill would have paired the mandate with affordability and charging support; this one did not.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the Senate's last two weeks, it was referred to the Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the ZEVs Act of 2022 on December 14, 2022, joined by a single cosponsor, Senator Whitehouse.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee the same day; no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers that sell mostly gas-powered vehicles and the oil refining and fuel-retail industry are better off, because no national zero-emission sales mandate or penalty system from this bill ever took effect. The committee that declined to act avoided a contested vote in a lame-duck session.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the ZEVs Act of 2022 on December 14, 2022.

for.name: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only cosponsor it attracted.

against.name: Sen. Tom Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the record shows no committee action after the December 14 referral, letting the bill die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held; the bill's only support came from two Senate Democrats — Merkley and Whitehouse — with no Republican or other cosponsors, and no opponent ever acted on the record.

industries.note: Automakers with established electric lineups would earn tradeable credits they could sell, while gas-heavy manufacturers would face credit purchases, civil penalties worth twice the missing credits' value, and a hard stop on new gas-car sales after 2035. The industry's dominant interest in this bill was avoiding the mandate, which put it against the clean-air benefit, though the electric leaders' interest ran the other way.

A 100% zero-emission requirement for new passenger vehicles from 2035 would steadily shrink future gasoline demand, cutting into refiners' and fuel retailers' core market. Their interest in stopping the bill ran directly against the public's interest in cleaner air.
Millions of additional electric vehicles would mean higher electricity sales and a buildout of charging infrastructure. This industry's gain arrives alongside the public's cleaner-air benefit.
